title: Trading the bass for administration
summary: Monk explains choosing administrative work over playing, to put something back and help children express themselves.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: In the process of all this, Monk, in the last five years, you've become less and less of a player and more and more of an active politician.

I find that very interesting, because people don't have a tendency to look at me any more as a jazz musician. They don't look at me as a bass player. And that sort of offends me, in a sense, because I think I am still. And I'm sure that I'm going to go back and pick up my instrument because that is my first love.
But you really have not been playing.

No, I haven't done any playing. Well, now...It was in spurts before but then it got to the point where I had to make a choice. I mean a total commitment to one or the other. And being the kind of person I am, I knew that was going to take place, but I had to make a total commitment to either this administrative business or this artistic business of playing. So...
But right now your interest, your total dedication, is more to the administrative...

The priority now is in administrative, because the other way felt to me -- and I really thought it out, I had to give it some serious thought -- to me, playing was...I could always go back and play anything, and perhaps be a better

musician when I got back to it because of the satisfaction I received doing what I'm doing. That's what the music is about anyhow, that's what we are about. That's how you express yourself, you express your experiences. And my experiences now, wasn't a selfish thing.

You see, I thought if I had gone to play my music, which I was entitled to, with anybody else, I couldn't do that and do this. And tolet this go...It's like, of all the efforts I felt like I put into this thing, of the administrative pulling together and that type of thing, if I can just save one person, one kid, if Ijust find it possible for one child to express himself, it's worth it all. It's really worth it all, and I see it that way.

I feel like it's my way of putting something back, because look how much I've gotten out of music. I've been sitting here talking about some things here just a minute, and I can't get it all in, all the wonderful things that's happened, that I received from being a musician, playing.

Now, the greatest thing that happened to me now is to put some of that back, to sort of feed back in, hopefully to pass on, to help make a continuum. Playing for myself is great; it is for any musician. It's the greatest thing in the world to have an outlet to express yourself, especially through something like music. But it's a selfish thing for me to think that way.

Because I wouldn't want to benefit by that, no matter how great a piece I would play, when they would applaud, they would applaud for me, they wouldn't be applauding for...all those other people wouldn't be sharing that, that I'm sharing...
You're building an audience through what you're doing now, in a particular way...
It'll work in its own way. I feel it would, it's better...
But if, as a by-product,after all this effort, you get jazz into places where there has never been jazz before, whether it's the Strip or whether it's some small town in Montana...
Well, if you really analyze what you're saying, this is what I'm counting on to happen to. The thing that I make happen on the Strip is going to make some things happen in Montana.
